newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Creditanstalt sale talks drag on.
newsitem.headline: Creditanstalt sale talks drag on.

text.p: Creditanstalt-Bankverein's sell-off entered a period of behind the scenes negotiations on Friday as two rival consortia worked frantically to finalise their bids for Austria's most traditional bank.

Consortium leaders Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian) and insurer EA-Generali confirmed they were still in the running to take over the state's 19.9 million Creditanstalt shares or 70 percent of ordinary voting stock.
"We are still interested and the consortium is still there," said a spokesman for the EA-Generali group.
The consortium, which includes Germany's Commerzbank and Italy's Banca Commerciale Italiana, was formed in 1994.
Despite enjoying the backing of Creditanstalt's management and conservative politicians, it has found little favour with successive Social Democrat finance ministers.

The group's latest bid foundered earlier this week because of its reluctance to take on all of the state's ordinary shares. The rejection came just weeks after First Austrian's exit from the consortium.
The savings bank later announced plans to set up a rival consortium and on Friday it was locked in talks to drum up financial backing for its bid.
"We have been in talks with many potential partners...We are preparing a bid but we don't know the make-up of the group yet," a source at the bank said.
Austrian media have reported that Belgium's Bacob bank could be among First Austrian's backers. Bacob has confirmed it has "an interest" in Creditanstalt.
First Austrian, one of Austria's top five banks, said it had set aside two billion schillings for its offer.

That falls well short of the 18 billion schillings the government had been targetting, based on an assessment last year by U.S. investment house J.P. Morgan, and the current market value of 13 billion schillings.
J.P. Morgan will update its assessment of the bank over the next two weeks and the finance ministry expects to pinpoint potential buyers within six to eight weeks.
The government is desperate to get the sale underway by the end of the year in order to bring in much needed revenue.
It is also painfully aware that the long-drawn out and very public privatisation has done little to enhance Austria's reputation abroad.
"It's obvious that this is doing nothing to help the Austrian financial market. That is why we are moving ahead with determination," said a finance ministry source.
